title: Around the World in 80 Days
tagline: Retrace Phileas Fogg's 1872 route — today's streets, Verne's guidebook.

chapters.title: Episode 1 · London — the bet
chapters.hook: How long would it take you to go all the way round the world? In 1872 nobody knew, and a man bet half his fortune on eighty days.

scenes.title: How long would it take you?
scenes.subtopic: T1 — the question, and today's answers
scenes.learning_goal: Know that a full circumnavigation now takes about 44 hours by scheduled flight and 90 minutes in orbit, and that in 1872 nobody knew the answer at all.

narration.script: How long would it take you to go all the way round the world? Today, about forty-four hours. In November twenty twenty-four, three men from Hong Kong went the whole way round on ordinary scheduled flights, on tickets anyone could buy. Higher up it is faster. The space station laps the planet every ninety minutes. The people on board watch sixteen sunrises a day. Now take all of that away. No aircraft. No radio. In eighteen seventy-two the honest answer was: nobody knew. So somebody turned it into a bet. Eighty days, half a fortune — and for the next hundred and fifty years, real people kept trying to beat him.

scenes.title: The people who actually raced it
scenes.subtopic: T2 — Train, Bly, Bisland, Huld, and the trophy
scenes.learning_goal: Know that real people have raced Fogg's fictional time for 150 years, that Nellie Bly won it in 72 days and met Verne on the way, and that the record now stands at 40 days by sea.

narration.script: Which is strange — because he never existed. The book came out, and people began treating a novel as a challenge. An American called George Francis Train insisted he had already done it, two years before the book, and spent the rest of his life saying so. Then in eighteen eighty-nine a New York reporter named Nellie Bly was given two days' notice, one bag and a ticket, and sent east. On the way she stopped at Amiens and met Jules Verne himself. She came home in seventy-two days, six hours and eleven minutes — and beat a man who did not exist. What she did not know is that a rival magazine had put a second woman on a train the same day, going the opposite way round. Elizabeth Bisland lost by four days. She also beat Fogg. It never stopped. In nineteen twenty-eight a Danish paper ran a competition in Verne's honour and sent the winner — a boy of fifteen — round the world with aircraft banned. Forty-four days. Twenty thousand people met him at Copenhagen station. And there is a sailing trophy named after Verne. The first time anyone won it, the time was seventy-nine days: under eighty by seventeen hours. It now stands at forty.

scenes.title: The man they were all chasing
scenes.subtopic: T3 — the wager, and what he is actually betting on
scenes.learning_goal: Know the terms of the wager and, more importantly, that Fogg is betting on the state of the world rather than on his own ability.

narration.script: So who were they racing? A man who spent the whole journey trying not to look at it. London, the second of October, eighteen seventy-two. In a club on Pall Mall, Phileas Fogg bets five other members half of everything he owns that he can go round the Earth and be back in that room in eighty days. Here is the part that matters. He is not betting on himself. He is betting on the planet — on whether the railways and steamers and canals finished in the last three years have actually joined up into one working machine. His friends think the world is still too big. He thinks it has just closed. And in eighteen seventy-two that was a genuinely open question. Which is why it is a bet and not a boast.

scenes.title: Why eighty — the year the world closed
scenes.subtopic: T4 — the four enablers, the telegraph, and the series promise
scenes.learning_goal: Know that four specific works finished between 1869 and 1872 made the eighty days arithmetic rather than fantasy, and that the last of them closed six weeks before Fogg leaves.

narration.script: Three years earlier the bet would have been impossible. Not hard. Impossible. May eighteen sixty-nine: two railways meet in Utah, and America has a line from coast to coast. November: the Suez Canal opens, and ships stop going round Africa. Eighteen seventy: India's railways join up across the subcontinent. September eighteen seventy-one: a tunnel opens under the Alps. And on the twenty-second of August, eighteen seventy-two — six weeks before Fogg walks out of his front door — the last stretch of telegraph wire is strung across Australia, and for the first time a message can go the whole way round the world and back. The last inhabited continent joins the network. The circuit closes. And then he sets off. That circuit is the route of this series. Eight episodes, one lap: the Channel and the Alps, the canal at Suez, the railway across India with a piece missing, the ports of the East, the Pacific, the line across America. And all the way round, the question Fogg is actually betting on. Had the world really closed? We are going to find out where it held — and where it very nearly didn't.

scenes.title: The largest city there had ever been
scenes.subtopic: T6 — London in 1872, and how new it was
scenes.learning_goal: Know that London was the largest city on earth and, more surprisingly, one of the newest — Fogg sets out from a modern city, not an old one.

narration.script: Fogg is setting out from the biggest city that had ever existed. London, eighteen seventy-one: three point nine million people. A quarter bigger than Beijing. Two-thirds bigger than Paris. Five times New York. The world's largest port. Twelve main railway termini — no other city had anything close. And an underground railway, the first anywhere, nine years old and already carrying nine and a half million people a year. Here is what people get wrong about Fogg's London. It was not old. The Embankment was two years old. His station was eight. The clock tower was thirteen. He set out from a brand-new city to find out whether the rest of the world had caught up.

scenes.title: Half a mile
scenes.subtopic: T7 — the three addresses, and the rule of this series
scenes.learning_goal: Know that Fogg's house, club and station sit within half a mile of each other, and that this episode walks that half mile.

narration.script: Everything left in this episode happens inside half a mile. Verne gives Fogg three addresses, all in the same corner of London. A house on Savile Row. A club on Pall Mall. A station at Charing Cross. He walks the first leg himself, and because he is the man he is, he counts it. Eleven hundred and fifty-one steps. About nine hundred metres. That is the whole of London he uses. A man about to go round the Earth spends his last day on it inside half a mile. So we are going to walk that half mile — because all three of those places turn out to be more interesting than the man who used them.

scenes.title: What a London club actually was
scenes.subtopic: T8 — the institution, and where 'blackballed' comes from
scenes.learning_goal: Know what a gentlemen's club was as an institution, how election by ballot worked, and that clubland was hundreds of buildings still standing today.

narration.script: Fogg makes the bet in a club. It is worth knowing what that word meant. Not a bar. A private house the size of a palace, where a few hundred men who agreed with each other could eat, read, write letters and in many of them sleep — all of it staffed, none of it for sale. You could not buy your way in. You were proposed, seconded, then voted on. Every member dropped a ball into a box: white to admit, black to reject. Enough black balls and you were out. That is where blackballed comes from. At its height London had more than four hundred of these places, most inside a few hundred metres of St James's and Pall Mall. This is the second leg of Fogg's walk, and almost every building on it is still standing.

scenes.title: The Reform — a party built as a palace
scenes.subtopic: T9 — why the building exists at all
scenes.learning_goal: Know that the Reform Club was founded in 1836 as a political counterweight to the Carlton, and what it is now.

narration.script: The room where Fogg makes his bet is, in real life, a political weapon. After the Reform Act of eighteen thirty-two, the Conservatives founded the Carlton Club, a few doors along Pall Mall. The other side wanted something to counter the machinations of the Carlton — their words — and in eighteen thirty-six they got it. So the room where a fictional Englishman bets half his fortune on the size of the world is the headquarters of a political faction, built to out-build the opposition down the street. It is still there, still a club. In nineteen eighty-one it became one of the first of the old clubs to admit women on equal terms. Its library, given book by book by its own members, runs to more than eighty-five thousand volumes.

scenes.title: Savile Row — 280 metres, and one word
scenes.subtopic: T10 — the street, the trade, and the word it lost
scenes.learning_goal: Know why the world's bespoke tailoring is named after one 280-metre street, that the word did not start there, and that the Row lost it at tribunal in 2008 and defended it with geography instead.

narration.script: Verne gives Fogg a house here — number seven. Here is what he does not tell you about the street. Two hundred and eighty metres, one block behind Regent Street. You can walk it in three minutes. The tailors arrived around eighteen-oh-three, following the army officers who already lived here — which is why the Savile Row shape comes from military uniform, not from fashion. The street will tell you the word bespoke was born here: cloth spoken for by a customer. It was not. The word is from seventeen fifty-five, fifty years before the first tailor arrived. And in two thousand and eight they lost it for real. The advertising regulator ruled that a machine-sewn suit made in Germany could still be called bespoke. Nobody owns the term. So the Row stopped defending the dictionary and started defending geography. Its own standard now demands a paper pattern cut for one person, fifty hours of hand work, three fittings — and a workshop within a hundred yards of this street. One last thing about Fogg living here. He leaves for three months with a single bag: two shirts and three pairs of stockings. He lived on the street where one suit takes fifty hours by hand — and he packed as though clothes did not exist.

scenes.title: No. 1 — where they decided what was still blank
scenes.subtopic: T11 — the Royal Geographical Society, six doors away
scenes.learning_goal: Know that the RGS ran the era's exploration from the top of Fogg's own street, and feel the irony against a man who crosses the world without looking at it.

narration.script: At the top of Fogg's street is the room where Britain worked out which parts of the world were still unmapped. From eighteen seventy the Royal Geographical Society had its headquarters at number one Savile Row — where expeditions to Africa, Asia and the South Pole were planned and argued over. In April eighteen seventy-four, David Livingstone's body lay in that building before it went to Westminster Abbey. Six doors down the same street, Verne had just put a man who bet he could go round the world without looking at any of it. One end of a three-minute street: the people who wanted to see everything. The other end: a man who crosses the planet and notices nothing. The Society sold the building to a tailor in nineteen twelve — partly because that firm had dressed so many of the explorers.

scenes.title: Charing Cross — the point London is measured from
scenes.subtopic: T12 — the datum, the Eleanor cross, and the departure
scenes.learning_goal: Know that all British road distances to London are measured from the Charing Cross statue, and what the Eleanor crosses were.

narration.script: He begins a journey round the world from the exact spot Britain measures every distance from. The third address. A bronze horseman at Charing Cross. Since the early eighteen hundreds it has been the point every road distance to London is counted from. When a sign in Scotland says London four hundred, it means this statue. Not the city. This statue. There is a stone cross in the station forecourt that looks medieval. It is Victorian, and it is in the wrong place. The real one stood where the horseman is now. It was the last of twelve. When Eleanor of Castile died in twelve ninety, her body was carried a hundred and eighty miles to Westminster, and Edward the First built a cross at every place it rested overnight. Charing was the final night, and its cross cost seven times any of the others. It came down in sixteen forty-seven, after standing three hundred and fifty-three years, and the parish sold the stone — forty-seven cartloads of it — for paving. Fogg's train leaves from a station built on that spot. And at a quarter to nine, a man walks onto a platform and starts measuring something rather larger.

scenes.title: A quarter to nine
scenes.subtopic: T13 — the departure, and the look ahead
scenes.learning_goal: Know how little he took and how little time he gave himself, and leave the episode wanting the next one.

narration.script: He gave himself ten minutes to pack for the planet. Fogg leaves the club at twenty-five past seven, tells his new servant they are going round the world and will start in ten minutes, and packs one carpet-bag: two shirts, three pairs of stockings, a mackintosh, a cloak, and a railway timetable. The train for Dover leaves at a quarter to nine. It is raining. Passepartout's watch is four minutes slow and set to London, and he has no intention of changing it for anybody. And somewhere behind them, in an empty house on Savile Row, a gas lamp is still burning that nobody turned off — which is going to be funny for about seventy-nine more days. Ahead of him: a boat across the Channel. A hole under the Alps that opened thirteen months ago. A canal three years old. A railway across India with a piece missing. An ocean that takes twenty-two days. And somewhere out on the Pacific, something quietly happens to the calendar that nobody on board notices. Eighty days. He has already gone.
